Guide tumor boundary decisions during live surgery
Same LED NIR concept as the kidney study
Can kidney study findings be quoted as proof the proposed sensor is ready for tumor boundary guidance?

missing: Target tissue types and tumor types, and the tumor-versus-healthy contrast expected
Sensor specification: wavelengths, LED power, detector, spectral resolution, acquisition speed
Probe geometry, size, sterilisation route and contact or non-contact operation
Intended clinical workflow: real-time decision timing, required spatial resolution and margin distance
Accuracy target: sensitivity and specificity needed against histopathology, and the acceptable false-negative rate at margins

requirements.status_reason: The enquiry can be assessed technically, but the kidney study cannot serve as proof of readiness for tumor boundary guidance. Organ, target, contrast mechanism, clinical endpoint and measurement conditions all differ, and no validation exists on the customer's own setup or in tumor tissue.
requirements.answer: No. The kidney study shows that the LED NIR concept can work for kidney tissue under the conditions it tested, but it does not establish that the sensor is ready for detecting tumor boundaries during live surgery. The next step is a laboratory feasibility study on tumor and surrounding tissue with histopathology as reference, followed by a bounded in vivo or ex vivo study only after go/no-go criteria are met.

inline.headline: Kidney study does not transfer as readiness evidence; run a lab-first feasibility study on tumor tissue before any in vivo use
inline.method: Start with diffuse reflectance LED NIR spectroscopy as the main method, with fluorescence and Raman as comparison options; assess whether tumor-to-healthy spectral contrast exists in the target tissue before optimising hardware
inline.probe: Fibre-coupled contact or near-contact probe with a defined working distance and fixed source-detector geometry, sized for a surgical instrument channel or hand-held use; design for a sterilisable, disposable tip if the concept proceeds
inline.install: Not yet defined. Feasibility work is bench-top first: fixed probe holder on an ex vivo tissue setup, then a controlled in vivo or intra-operative pilot only after lab go/no-go
inline.fiber: Multi-fibre bundle or fibre pair with defined numerical aperture and source-detector separation, matched to LED output and spectrometer or photodiode detector; fibre choice depends on the wavelength range and required depth sensitivity
inline.test_against: Histopathology of matched tumor, margin and healthy-tissue samples, with pixel-to-biopsy registration; ideally a blinded comparison with an independent pathologist
inline.not_final_because: The kidney study is a different organ and target, no tumor-tissue data exist, the customer's own setup is unvalidated, the reference standard and clinical endpoint are undefined, and no in vivo or intra-operative data exist

problems.text: Treating the kidney study as proof of readiness assumes results transfer across organs, tissue types and clinical tasks. Kidney tissue differs in optical properties, perfusion and background from tumor tissue, so the kidney contrast does not predict tumor-boundary contrast.
Assuming the LED NIR concept is sufficient for the new use. Its signal depends on the target chromophores or scattering contrast present in the tumor. That contrast is unknown and must be measured.
The kidney study's conditions (in vivo or ex vivo, perfusion state, number of subjects, reference method, statistics) are unknown from the enquiry and must be checked before any finding is quoted.

Clinical use during live surgery introduces motion, bleeding, fluid, lighting and probe-contact variability that a static study does not capture. Each needs to be tested before performance can be claimed.

Boundary decisions need spatial resolution and a defined margin distance. Point or small-area measurements may not resolve a tumor edge; the required resolution must be set against the clinical margin criterion.
Using the kidney study as regulatory or clinical evidence of readiness would be inappropriate. The claim cannot be supported without the validation steps described below.

methods.why: Matches the kidney study concept and is simple, fast and fibre-compatible. Its value for tumor boundaries depends on whether a measurable tumor-to-healthy contrast exists at the chosen wavelengths.

methods.method: Autofluorescence spectroscopy at the excitation used by the sensor
methods.why: Tumor tissue often shows altered metabolic and structural fluorescence. It can add contrast where reflectance is weak, and it can be tested with the same probe and fibre geometry.

methods.method: Raman spectroscopy with a fibre probe
methods.why: Gives molecular specificity for tissue classification. It is slower and needs careful background and fluorescence rejection, so it fits as a reference or confirmatory method.

methods.method: Fluorescence imaging with an exogenous contrast agent
methods.why: Can give strong tumor contrast but adds drug, regulatory and workflow requirements. Consider only if label-free methods fail to separate tumor from healthy tissue.

methods.method: Hyperspectral imaging across the visible to NIR range
methods.why: Useful for mapping spatial contrast and selecting wavelengths during development. It is not an in-line probe concept, so it is better as a laboratory tool than as the sensor.

questions.q: What are the tumor types, tissue sites and the healthy tissue the surgeon must distinguish?
questions.why: Contrast depends on the specific tumor and background tissue, so the study design and wavelengths depend on this.

questions.q: What decision does the sensor support, and what is the required accuracy, sensitivity and specificity at the margin?
questions.why: Defines the go/no-go criteria and whether point measurement or imaging is needed.

questions.q: What spatial resolution and margin distance are clinically required?
questions.why: Determines probe size, measurement spot, scanning strategy and the relevant reference-standard sampling.

questions.q: What were the kidney study's conditions: in vivo or ex vivo, sample size, reference method, statistical analysis, and which results are publicly reported?
questions.why: Needed to judge what can and cannot be quoted, and to replicate the approach fairly.

questions.q: Is there any existing tumor-tissue spectral data from the customer, a collaborator or the literature?
questions.why: Could reduce the lab study scope by identifying candidate wavelengths before new measurements.

questions.q: What is the intended operating environment: contact or non-contact, hand-held or robotic, and the sterilisation route?
questions.why: Affects probe geometry, working distance, fibre choice and the test conditions needed.

questions.q: What is the regulatory pathway and timeline?
questions.why: Determines the evidence level required and the sequence of lab, pre-clinical and clinical steps.

experiment.objective: Determine whether LED NIR and complementary optical methods give a measurable and reproducible contrast between tumor and surrounding healthy tissue, measured with the intended probe concept, against histopathology as reference.
steps: Define the clinical question, target tissues, required accuracy and the margin criterion with the customer.
Obtain the kidney study data or protocol to confirm its conditions and identify what does not transfer.
Collect ex vivo tumor, margin and healthy tissue samples under ethics and sourcing approval, with matched sampling for histopathology.
Acquire broadband reflectance and autofluorescence spectra at fixed probe geometry across the candidate LED wavelengths, and record a reference Raman spectrum on a subset.
Build a spectral dataset with pixel-to-biopsy registration, then assess tumor-to-healthy contrast, signal-to-noise and inter-sample variability.
Select the candidate wavelength set and combination (for example reflectance plus autofluorescence) and build a simple classifier with cross-validation and a held-out blinded test set.
Test the probe under surgical-like conditions: motion, blood, saline or fluid, ambient light and repeated sterilisation or handling.
Assess calibration stability and drift over a representative working session.
Write a go/no-go report against the pre-defined criteria, and only then plan a bounded in vivo or intra-operative pilot.
references: Histopathology as the reference standard for tumor versus healthy tissue classification
Published guidance on reporting diagnostic accuracy for optical and spectroscopic tissue classification (for example STARD-style reporting)
Published fibre-optic reflectance and fluorescence spectroscopy studies of tumor tissue in the relevant organ, to be identified by the team
Customer's kidney LED NIR study, to be checked for conditions and reported results
experiment.go_no_go: Go to in vivo or intra-operative pilot only if: a reproducible tumor-to-healthy spectral contrast is shown on independent samples; the blinded classifier meets the pre-agreed sensitivity and specificity at the margin criterion; the probe performs within specification under surgical-like conditions; and calibration drift stays within the agreed limit over a session. Otherwise stop, or redesign wavelengths, method or probe.

multispectral.combination: LED NIR diffuse reflectance combined with autofluorescence (and Raman as a reference on a subset) using the same probe geometry, with wavelength selection from the lab spectral data
multispectral.why: Reflectance and fluorescence probe different tissue properties (scattering and absorption versus endogenous fluorophores), so combining them can improve tumor contrast and reduce false positives from either channel alone. Raman provides molecular specificity for confirming the classification during development.

assumptions: The customer's kidney study is accurately described in the enquiry and its findings are not yet reviewed by AFS.
No tumor-tissue optical data exists for the customer's sensor.
The sensor is intended to be used in human surgery, so regulatory and clinical evidence will be required beyond the feasibility study.
The customer's LED source and detector are representative of the proposed sensor, though their specifications are not yet stated.
Histopathology is accepted as the reference standard for the tumor-boundary question.
No in vivo, intra-operative or patient-data use is planned before lab go/no-go is met.
